build: G64 disk image: a 101-byte boot program and a 1,265-byte fast loader as files, and the game in raw sectors, its $4000-$CFFF EORed with $C9; one load, entered at $0F80

exclude: runtime: zero page, the game's variables, zeroed by cold_start and written as it runs
runtime: the game's tables of tanks, bullets, grenades and soldiers ($020E-$03ED); at the hand-over pages 2 and 3 still hold the loader's leftovers
runtime: the map window's characters, 64 rows of 32 built by draw_map_row; at the hand-over it still holds the loader, which nothing runs again
runtime: the map window's colours (it runs on to $13FF, over the start-up code at $0F80, once play begins)
runtime: sprite frame $40, the empty frame, cleared by cold_start

runtime: the multiplexer's bucket table ($7A80), the 36 moving objects ($7B00-$7BD5), the marker list ($7BDD-$7CCD), the map objects' slots ($7CE5-$7D6F), the blast and gun lists and the big explosion queue ($7D73-$7E2B)
runtime: the music driver's state for its three voices, cleared by start_tune
runtime: the sound effects' slots and the voices' effect flags, written by start_effect_voice and effect_update
runtime: the processor's vectors, set by the game ($FFFA NMI, $FFFE IRQ); nothing else is loaded here

comments.text: The opening sequence's own sprite shapes, 16 frames of 64 bytes, swapped into $5040-$543F (frames $41-$50) for the intro by swap_intro_sprites and back afterwards: the pieces of the aircraft it shows, each built from several sprites, with two-frame animations (intro_anim_a, intro_anim_b).

The game's first instruction, jumped to by the loader at $040C. Masks interrupts, banks the ROMs out ($01=$35), silences CIA 1's interrupts, sets both CIAs' data directions, puts the video chip in bank 1 ($DD00=$97), silences three SID voices, starts CIA 1 timer A, initialises the music driver (stop_music, then tune 0 via start_tune), plays the opening sequence (intro_sequence), then zeroes the game's variables, clears 36 bytes at $7B48 and fills 128 at $7A80 with $FF, calls reset_game_vars and install_irq, fills the screen at $4000-$43E7 with character $FF and colour RAM with 0, sets the pointers at $4FF8 to $FF, clears $5000-$503F, selects screen $4000 and characters $4800 ($D018=$02), turns the screen on and jumps to title_loop. Runs once per power-on; the code here is overwritten by buffers once play starts.

The opening sequence played once after loading: points the IRQ at intro_irq ($1253, music only), copies 47 sprite registers from intro_sprite_regs (among them a blue background, 6), swaps in the intro's sprite shapes with swap_intro_sprites, fills the screen with character 0 and colour RAM with 8, sets the eight sprite pointers from intro_sprite_ptrs, starts tune 2, then moves the sprites in stages (each stage waits a frame with wait_frame): scrolls them left until their X high bits clear and sprite 0 is left of 136, then scrolls the background (scroll_x_step, scroll_y_step, draw_intro_rows) for 12 rows, moves the sprites down until sprite 0 reaches line 212, plays effect 9, slides them along intro_slide_table for 114 frames (effect 20 at step 64), then wipes the screen with a raster split that grows by two lines a frame. Ends by swapping the sprite shapes back (swap_intro_sprites) and calling restore_charset.
Raster interrupt used only during intro_sequence: saves A, X and Y, calls the music driver's frame routine at music_tick, acknowledges the video chip's interrupt and returns.
Moves the eight sprites one pixel right (increments $D000, $D002 ... $D00E). Called once a frame from one stage of intro_sequence.

Waits for the raster to pass line 256 and come back (bit 7 of $D011 low, then high), counts the frame in zpa_2F and returns its low bit in A with Z set on even frames. Used by intro_sequence to pace its stages and to animate on alternate frames.
Flips the pointers of sprites 0 and 4 between frames $41/$43 and $42/$44, a two-frame animation of the intro's first pair of sprites.
Flips the pointers of sprites 5, 6 and 7 between frames $4B-$4D and $4E-$50, the intro's second animation.
Moves the screen's fine vertical scroll ($D011 bits 0-2) up one pixel with the screen kept on; when it wraps past 0, counts a whole row in zpa_4F.
Adds the speed zpa_46/zpa_47 (8.8 fixed point) to the fine horizontal scroll in $D016; when the scroll passes a character width, counts a column in zpa_50 (downwards).

Swaps the 1 KB at $5040-$543F, the game's sprite frames $41-$50, with the 1 KB at $0800-$0BFF (four pages through the pointers zpa_42/zpa_44), byte for byte. Called before and after the intro, so the intro's own sprite shapes, kept at $0800, take the place of the game's for the intro and give it back afterwards.

Redraws the intro's scrolling ground: from the row that zpa_4F has reached, copies rows of 40 characters taken cyclically from a 20-byte pattern at $4CE8 (wrapping at 19, starting at the column offset zpa_50), down the screen at $4000 until the address reaches $43E8. Rewrites its own operand at $1340/$1341 to step through the pattern.
The low byte of the pattern address in draw_intro_rows' LDA, rewritten by that routine as it steps through the 20-byte pattern.
The high byte of the same address, moved on by draw_intro_rows when the low byte wraps.
47 bytes copied to the video chip's $D000-$D02E at the start of the intro: sprite positions, high bits, control, enable, colours.
Eight sprite pointers stored at $43F8-$43FF for the intro's sprites.

114 per-frame steps subtracted from both the X and the Y of every sprite by one stage of intro_sequence. They run positive, then zero, then negative, in three rounds that shrink, so the sprites hop up and left and drop back down and right three times.

The attract loop, entered after the intro and after every game. Sets zpa_A9 and zpa_AB to $FF (attract mode) and cycles its screens, each a routine that returns with the carry clear when the player starts a game: $1E81, $20CA, $1EE4, then the demo game at demo_play ($1522), $B793 when the demo ran its full length, $1631, $20CA again and $1EB8, with $B78F between some of them. A clear carry from any of them goes on to game_start.

Starts a game: clears zpa_A9, resets the game's variables (reset_game_vars), calls $22E3, copies zpa_93 to zpa_1D, starts tune 2 through play_tune, sets zpa_8B to $98 and zpa_8C to $98 for two players or $93 for one (zpa_12 is the number of players), calls $39DB with zpa_12 forced to 2, clears zpa_1C and $7B49, sets zpa_39 to $FF and calls $231B for each player in the game. Falls into main_loop.

The game's main loop, two halves per pass. Each half starts by copying the 16-bit scroll position zpa_0C/zpa_0D into zpa_40/zpa_41, reading it until the low byte holds still because the interrupt changes it. The first half calls $393A, $233A, $290A, spawn_from_route ($194E), $1A1F, $263C and $39BD, jumps to $C77C when zpa_AD is negative, then calls update_shots and $C642. The second half calls $B54B, $39D1, $C02F, $28A4, $28D6, $39BD, update_shots, $BA25, $BE1E, $C376, $39BD, $CD23, $BC90, $B8F7 and $BC62. The loop ends when $390E returns with Z set, or when zpa_38 and zpa_39 are both negative and zpa_8B plus zpa_8C makes $26; it then calls $CA37 and jumps to $C7E4.

The attract mode's demo: plays the game by itself from one of nine starting points. Resets the variables, calls $81C3 with $92F9, takes the next pair from demo_starts (zpa_0A steps through them two bytes at a time and wraps after nine) into zpa_4F/zpa_50, a number of map rows to scroll. With a pair of 0 it draws the screens through $1CD1, $1CC8 and $1CBF and skips the scroll; otherwise it draws a map row with $7F80 and moves the scroll position on 8 for each row, row by row, until the count runs out. During attract mode it notes in zpa_52 whether 50 frames passed. Then shows the screen ($1E57 with $15, $13, $EC, $14 and $1CD1) and the message at $21EE through $2298, and returns with the carry set.

Nine pairs of bytes, each a 16-bit count of map rows that demo_play scrolls through before the demo starts: $0039, $00FC, $0139, $02A6, $02FA, $03A5, $0470, $04F7 and $0735. None is 0, so the branch in demo_play for a pair of 0 never runs.
The high bytes of demo_starts' row counts, read one byte on.
The background colour ($D021) for each demo start, read by $1631 with the same index zpa_0A that demo_play advanced (two bytes a start, the first of each pair used).

One of the attract screens: calls $1D07 and returns with the carry clear if it did; otherwise shows screen $EA ($1E57), draws through $1CC8, shows screen $16, sets the background colour from demo_backgrounds and the two multicolours to 9 and 13, and calls $1F21; if that returns with the carry set, sets zpa_AA to $FF and calls $204C.

Puts every per-game variable back to its starting value: zpa_38 and zpa_39 to $FF, the scroll position zpa_0C/zpa_0D to zpa_4B plus $100, and a long list of zero-page and $7Bxx/$02xx variables to 0; $7B6C/$7B6D to $A0, $7B90/$7B91 to 10 and 9, zpa_17/zpa_18 to $80/$E4, zpa_94/zpa_95 (the spawn list pointer) to $ACA7, zpa_AE, zpa_DE and $7DE3 to $FF, and the 20 bytes at zpf_71 to $FF. Called at power-on, at the start of each game and of each demo.
Stores the tune number in A in zpa_A3 and, when bit 6 of zpa_9C is set (music on), starts it through the music driver's $E09A.

Moves the bullets, which are drawn into the background characters rather than as sprites. Runs once for each frame since the last call, at most 7 steps at once. Each of 15 slots at $02C5+x with bit 7 set is a live bullet: its low six bits are the map row, $02D4+x the column in quarter-cells, $02E3+x the quarter-row inside the cell, $02F2+x the range left, $033F+x its direction (0-7, an index into shot_dx and shot_dy). The bullet's old cell gets its saved character back ($0330+x), in the map row (pointer table $C87F) and, when the row is on screen (within 22 rows of zpa_4C), in the screen row (pointer table $C97F). The bullet then moves, ends when its range runs out, it leaves the window of map rows kept, or the new cell's character has bit 6 set in char_colours ($7E80, solid) unless the slot's $034E+x is set (the shoot-through power-up). Otherwise the new cell's character is saved and copied into custom character $F0+x at $4F80+x*8 with a two-pixel dot drawn in by shot_masks and shot_bits, in a colour chosen by the character's bits 4-5 in char_colours, and $F0+x is written into the map and the screen.
16 AND masks, four per colour group, each clearing one two-bit multicolour pixel ($3F, $CF, $F3, $FC): update_shots picks one by the bullet's column within the cell.
16 OR values beside shot_masks, giving the bullet's pixel colour on each kind of background: $00 (background colour), $C0/$30/$0C/$03 (colour 3), $80/$20/$08/$02 (colour 2) or $FF.
The column step for each of the eight directions, 0 up, then clockwise: 0, +1, +1, +1, 0, -1, -1, -1.
The row step for the same eight directions: -1, -1, 0, +1, +1, +1, 0, -1.

Starts enemies as the screen scrolls. Reads the next entry of the route list at zpa_94/zpa_95: a 16-bit scroll position and a pointer. When the scroll position zpa_40/zpa_41 has passed it, moves the list on 4 bytes and reads the group the pointer names: each enemy is four bytes (type times two, slot data, a value less one, a flags byte) and goes into the first free slot of 16 at $7B58; the group ends at a 0, and bytes below 8 are skipped. Every fourth enemy started is given an item to drop, taken in turn from the pairs at item_cycle ($B53C). A pointer with a high byte of 0 is a scroll marker instead: it is recorded in the first free slot of eight at $7BF5.

The soldiers' decisions, run when at least 10 frames have passed since the last time (zpa_97) and zpa_AC is 0. For each of the 16 enemy slots in use ($7B58+x non-zero): looks up the map cell under the soldier (row from its Y, $7B58, through the row pointers at $C8FF; column from its X, $7B10/$7B34) and sets $03DD+x to $FF when the cell's low four bits are $E (water), 0 otherwise. A soldier whose state $036D+x has bit 7 set is dying: from $E0 on it steps through the frames in enemy_death_frames, and at step 21 its slot is freed. Otherwise, at most every 10 frames per soldier ($039D+x), it picks the nearer living player (zpa_38/zpa_39 are 0 for a living player; the distance is half the Y difference plus the X difference), works out which of 16 directions that player lies in by comparing the two differences, turns it into one of eight facings with dir16_to_dir8, and stores the facing in $03AD+x. A soldier whose flags $03BD+x have bit 7 clear also takes the facing as its sprite frame ($49 plus the facing, or $E2 plus the facing in water). When the facing has not changed since its last turn and a random number (random) is below fire_chance for its kind, it attacks: a kind with the high nibble 0 of $03BD+x fires a bullet (enemy_fire), the other kinds throw a grenade through $C9AB (kind $10 only when the targeted player's zpa_36 is non-zero, with $20 in A).
16 bytes turning the octant arithmetic in enemy_think (four sign and size bits) into one of the eight facings 0-7, 0 being up and the rest clockwise.

Four thresholds for a random byte, one per kind of soldier ($036D+x bits 0-1): 0 (never), $20, $80 and $FF (almost always). Byte $1C30 itself is also used as the general threshold where the facing alone counts; it is cleared by reset_game_vars.
21 sprite frames shown in turn by a dying soldier, one a step: pairs of $51, $55, $59, $5C, $60, $64, $68, $6B, $51, $55, then $40.

Starts an enemy bullet from soldier X: finds a free bullet slot among slots 6-14 (slots 0-5 are the players'), and gives it the soldier's facing as its direction, the range from shot_range, and a starting cell worked out from the soldier's position plus the offsets in shot_start_x and shot_start_y for that facing. Records the soldier's slot in $0301+y and clears the shoot-through flag $034E+y.
For each of the eight facings, the X offset in quarter-cells from a soldier's sprite to where its bullet starts.
For each of the eight facings, the Y offset in pixels from a soldier's sprite to where its bullet starts.
Fills the map with the character and colour in X and Y (fill_rows) with the extra steps $1E67 before and $1E74 after.
The same fill with $1E74 before and $1E67 after.

Fills 23 rows of the map, starting at the row $1E50 returns, with the character in X (map rows, pointers at $C87F) and the colour in Y (colour rows, pointers at $C8FF), 32 cells a row, wrapping round the 64-row window. Used to blank the play area between screens.
Plays the scroll script at $1D79 through run_scroll_script.
Plays the scroll script at $1DA8 through run_scroll_script.
Plays the scroll script at $1DDF through run_scroll_script.
Plays the scroll script at $1D3F through run_scroll_script.
Plays the scroll script at $1E0E through run_scroll_script.

Hands the interrupt a script of per-frame scroll steps (pointer in zpa_A7/zpa_A8) and waits until the interrupt has played it and cleared zpa_A8. Returns with the carry clear when zpa_A9 came back as $7F (a player pressed fire during attract mode; zpa_A9 and zpa_A8 are cleared), otherwise with the carry set and zpa_4B cleared.

Five scripts for run_scroll_script, each a list of signed per-frame scroll steps ended by $7F: at $1D3F, $1D79, $1DA8, $1DDF and $1E0E. They speed the picture up, hold a steady speed, and slow it down, for the title sequence's moving screens.
The fourth scroll script, from $1DDF, continued: run_scroll_script reads it from the indexed base here.
The end of the fifth scroll script, from $1E0E.
Waits until the interrupt has finished any coarse scroll it was asked for (zpa_23 back to 0) and returns the top map row zpa_4C in A.
Waits for the interrupt to be idle (zpa_23 = 0), then adds A to the top map row zpa_4C, modulo 64, and stores it in zpa_4C and zpa_93. The title sequence uses it to jump the view by whole screens.
Moves the top map row zpa_4C (and zpa_93) on by 23 rows, one screen, modulo 64.
Moves the top map row zpa_4C (and zpa_93) back by 23 rows, one screen, modulo 64.

First screen of the attract sequence: blanks the map, plays scroll script b; then the high-score table falls in (title_letters_fall with zpa_AA = $FF); then, on a black background, draws the double-height title lettering (draw_big_title) and plays scroll scripts c and e with multicolours 8 and 9. Each step returns at once with the carry clear when a player pressed fire.

Attract screen: blanks the map, plays scroll script b, then draws the credits (draw_credits), restores the game's character set (restore_charset) and plays scroll scripts c and e with multicolours 11 and 15. Returns at once with the carry clear when a player pressed fire.

Attract screen: blanks the map, plays scroll script b, restores the game's character set, copies the title font (copy_title_font), prints the credits at $21EE one screen up (print_text), then plays scroll scripts c and e with multicolours 9 and 13. Returns with the carry clear when a player pressed fire, once the scroll script running at the time has ended.
Plays scroll script c and, unless a player pressed fire, scroll script e: the picture slides in and away again.

Writes the high-score table at $2108 (ten rows of 23 characters, "1ST 100000 IKARI" and the rest) into the map one screen up, five cells in, every other row, skipping spaces ($20) and blanks ($E0), each in colour 13; then copies the title font and moves the view back down. Despite its name it draws the scores; the credits are the text at $21EE.
Copies 504 bytes of character shapes from $AAD7 to $4E00-$4FF7 (characters $C0-$FE of the set at $4800): the letters and digits used by the title, high-score and message screens.

Builds the double-height title lettering: copies $F500-$F847 into the character set at $4800 with every byte written twice (each source row becomes two rows, 105 characters), then copies 18 rows of 32 cells from the map at $F848 (characters) and $FA48 (colours) into the map window, the first row blank, three rows below the top.

Starts the ten sprites of the "WARRIORS" style title letters (positions from title_sprite_x/title_sprite_xhi, colours, pointers $89-$92 and Y from title_sprite_y) and moves them down frame by frame by the steps in the scroll script that starts at $1DFC, until it ends. Returns with Z set when attract mode was left (zpa_A9 = $FF).

Starting X positions, frames, colours and Y positions of the ten title sprites, in five tables of ten read by title_letters_fall: X low bytes at $2098, X high bytes at $20A2, Y at $20AC, pointers at $20B6, colours at $20C0.
The ten title sprites' X high bytes.
The ten title sprites' Y positions.
The ten title sprites' frames ($89-$92: IKARI and the pieces of "Warriors").
The ten title sprites' colours.
Each frame, moves the ten title sprites four pixels left and five of them one pixel down, until $7B28 is cleared; then clears their Y positions. Returns with Z set when attract mode was left.

The text written by draw_credits and by print_text at $21EE, in the game's character codes (letters $C1-$DA, digits $F0-$F9, space $20 or $E0): the ten rows of the high-score table as first loaded ("1ST 100000 IKARI" down to "10TH 010000 IKARI"), then "IKARI WARRIORS", "(C) ELITE SYSTEMS LTD 1988", "WRITTEN BY JOHN TWIDDY", "GRAPHICS BY PAUL WALKER, RORY GREEN, KAREN TRUEMAN, JOHN HARRISON" and "MUSIC BY JASON BROOKE". In the print_text part a byte below $80 is a number of columns to skip, $FE starts the next character run, $FF ends a row and 0 ends the text.

The first digit of the first entry's score (each entry is 23 bytes: its rank in six characters, the score in six digits, two spaces and a name of nine letters); enter_high_score compares scores from here.
The second digit of the first entry's score, compared next.
The third digit of the first entry's score.
The fourth digit of the first entry's score, the last enter_high_score compares (the last two are always 0).
The fourth to tenth rows of the high-score table: "4TH 070000 IKARI" down to "10TH 010000 IKARI".
The credits print_text writes on the title pages: "IKARI WARRIORS", "(C) ELITE SYSTEMS LTD 1988", "WRITTEN BY JOHN TWIDDY", the four graphic artists and "MUSIC BY JASON BROOKE".

Prints text into the map at the top row zpa_4C and down, from the address in X (low) and Y (high), in the format of hiscore_text: a byte below $80 moves the column, $FF ends the row, $FE skips one byte and 0 ends.

The scroll that leads into a game: blanks the map and plays scroll script d, restores the character set, sets the background to orange (8), puts the view at row 0, draws the first rows of the route ($3993), blanks the screen below, plays scroll script b and calls $398F.

Puts player X at the start: Y position $EE (zpa_1B+x), $58 into zpa_A5+x, the dead flag zpa_38+x, the tank flag zpa_55+x and the power-ups zpa_CA, zpa_E2, zpa_E4 and zpa_E6 for that player to 0, 99 bullets and 50 grenades (BCD, zpa_6D+x and zpa_6F+x).

Reads each living player's fire button every second frame and works out shooting and throwing. Fire held in zpa_10+x bit 4 clear is pressed. On the press itself (counter zpa_3E+x at 0) the player fires a bullet at once: out of a tank, one bullet from the 99 (BCD, zpa_6D+x), into a free slot of 0-2 (player 1, who may also use 3-5 in a one-player game) or 3-5 (player 2), through player_shot; in a tank, a shell through throw_grenade with $80. Holding fire counts on; at the ninth count, while no grenade is already flying and no tank is being boarded, the player in a tank climbs out ($2A64), and a player on foot next to an empty tank (within 16 pixels across and 32 down of one of the four in $020E-$0211) starts boarding it; otherwise a grenade is thrown (throw_grenade with 0) and zpa_5D+x is set to 24. Releasing fire resets the counter.

Throws a grenade (A = 0) or fires a tank shell (A = $80) for player X into one of that player's two slots at $7B4C (X or X+2); returns with the carry set if both are busy or the player has none left. A grenade costs one of the BCD count zpa_6F+x, a shell one of zpa_E0+x. The slot takes the player's facing zpa_31+x, the blast power-up zpa_E6+x ($02AC) and the shoot-through power-up zpa_E4+x ($02B9), a range from grenade_range by facing, and a start position offset from the player by grenade_start_x and grenade_start_y. A shell fired with the long-range power-up (zpa_E2+x) takes its range from grenade_range_long instead, but indexed by the slot number in Y rather than the facing: a slip that gives player 1's shells $40 and player 2's $2E or $32 whatever their direction. Plays sound 7 for a grenade, 2 for a shell.
X offsets from the player to where a grenade (first eight, one per facing) or a shell (last eight) starts.
Y offsets from the player to where a grenade (first eight) or a shell (last eight) starts.
How long a grenade or shell flies for each of the eight facings (0 up, then clockwise): $30 up, right and left, $35 down, $26 on the upward diagonals and $29 on the downward ones.

The longer ranges of a tank's shells with the long-range power-up, meant per facing like grenade_range ($40 up, right and left, $46 down, $2E and $32 on the diagonals), but read by slot number (see throw_grenade), so a shell gets $40 from slot 0 or 2 (player 1) and $2E or $32 from slot 1 or 3 (player 2). A grenade thrown on foot never uses them.
How far a bullet travels for each of the eight facings: $30 up and down, $36 sideways, $22-$26 diagonally. Used for the players' and the soldiers' bullets.
The longer bullet ranges with the long-range power-up: $48 up and down, $4F sideways, $32-$38 diagonally.

Fires player X's bullet into bullet slot Y: its range from shot_range, or from shot_range_long when zpa_E2 is set, but read without the player index, so both players' bullets go by player 1's power-up; its direction from the player's facing; its start cell from the player's position plus player_shot_x and player_shot_y for that facing (none if that would be left of the map). Plays sound 0 and copies the player's shoot-through power-up zpa_E4+x into the slot.
X offsets in quarter-cells from the player to the start of a bullet, one per facing.
Y offsets in pixels from the player to the start of a bullet, one per facing.
Turns a position (zpa_BF in pixels across, zpa_C0 down) into a map cell (column zpa_B9, row zpa_BA) and calls $CCEB with A and X passed on in zpa_F2 and zpa_F3; Y is kept.
Blows up tank X: sets up an explosion through $BD49 at the tank's position (when a slot is free, with timers $40 and $FD), plays sound 9, and clears the tank's entry in $020E and $7B68.
Copies the game's character shapes from $FC48-$FEFF into $4800-$4AB7, undoing what the title screens wrote over them.

Works out where tank slot X is on screen, if it is within 18 rows of the top: zpa_C0 = its Y in pixels from its map row ($7DD7+x), zpa_BF = its X from its column ($7DD3+x). Returns with the carry set when it is off screen.
SEC and RTS that nothing calls, left between tank_screen_pos and update_guns.

Runs the four gun positions at $7DCF+x every 16 frames (a slot's value is its kind; 0 is empty, and a slot whose map row is more than 57 rows from zpa_5F is dropped). A kind of 3 or more (a mortar pit) checks every 30 frames for a living player below it within 90 pixels, then fires three shells upward-spread into free enemy bullet slots (directions 3-5, range $30, sound 13). Kinds 1 and 2 are turrets drawn in characters: each picks the nearer living player below it, aims left, down or right (a player more than 96 pixels away is ignored), redraws its barrel in the character set from turret_left_gfx ($AA47, kind 1) or turret_right_gfx ($AA8F, kind 2) when the aim changes, and when the aim is unchanged and a random byte is below $C0 fires one bullet in that direction (range $30) from the offsets in turret_shot_x.

For each turret aim (0 left, 1 down, 2 right), the last byte of its 24 bytes of character shapes in the turret graphics, then (from $2806) the offset of the turret's characters in the set, then (from $2809) the X offsets of its bullet, three for kind 2 and three for kind 1.
The offset of each turret aim's characters in the character set.
The X offsets of a turret's bullet for each aim, three for kind 2 and three for kind 1.

Draws rubble over a rectangle of the map after an explosion: for slot X of the blast list at $7DC3, from map row $7DB1+x to $7DA5+x and columns $7D9F+x to $7DAB+x, writes random rubble characters from crater_chars with colours from crater_colours into the map, and into the screen too when the row is visible (through $B8B3). The rubble piece $0D is followed by character $C6 in colour 8. Clears the slot when done.
16 rubble characters picked at random by make_crater.
The colour of each of the 16 rubble characters.
Every 20 frames, frees the route markers at $7BF5 (24 slots) whose row has scrolled 54 to 59 rows past zpa_5F.
Every 20 frames, frees the blast-list slots at $7DC3 (6 slots) whose last row has scrolled 58 to 61 rows past zpa_5F.
The two colours a mine flashes between when a player comes near (update_mines): 10 and 8 as colour RAM values, red and black in multicolour.

Every 8 frames: works out the scroll position of the bottom of the screen; drops any of the four tank slots ($020E-$0211) that has fallen below it; when the scroll position passes the next entry of tank_list (index zpa_4E), places that empty tank in a free slot ($40, flashing "IN"); then for each tank in use puts it on screen as a sprite when it is within 32 pixels above to 6 below the view (setting its sprite X, Y and colour 12), or takes it off. A tank with a hit time in $026E+x explodes 100 frames after it (tank_destroyed) and meanwhile shows the smoking frames $DF-$E1 by zpa_CE; an unhit one alternates its frame from tank_in_frames.

The twelve empty tanks placed along the route, four bytes each: X position (16 bits) and the scroll position at which it appears (16 bits): X $086 and $0CA at $021C, $061 at $04C2, $0AC at $08D7, $09B at $0C7A, $04A at $0E68 and $0E89, $088, $0A9 and $0C8 at $1336, $09D at $1BA5 and $113 at $2753; then $FFFF ends the list.
The high byte of the first tank's X position; each entry of tank_list is four bytes.
The first tank's scroll position (16 bits).
The high byte of the first tank's scroll position, read with the other three bytes of each entry.
Eight frames shown in turn by an empty tank: six of $C6 and two of $DE, which makes the "IN" sign flash.

Player X climbs out of the tank: the tank is put back in a free tank slot where the player was, with the player's shells (zpa_E0+x), its damage state (zpa_53+x) and hit time (zpa_CA+x), and is shown with frame $C6. The player steps one pixel down, the tank flags zpa_36+x, zpa_5B+x and zpa_CA+x are cleared, the sprite frame is set again (player_frame) and zpa_59+x is set to $FF.

Chooses player X's sprite frame ($7B6C+x) and colour ($7B90+x). In a tank: the turret frame for the facing and the tread step from tank_frame_base and tank_frames, or the smoking frames $DF-$E1 when hit, flashing colour 1 while damage zpa_53+x is below $20. On foot: the walking frame from walk_frame_base and walk_frames, or the throwing frame from throw_frames while zpa_6A+x is set, flashing colour 1 every 8 frames while zpa_A5+x (the start-of-life invulnerability) runs. The normal colours come from player_colours ($B78D).
Three frames ($DF, $E0, $E1) of a smoking tank, shown while its countdown runs: after a grenade hit, or after its fuel ran out.
For each facing, where its walking frames start in walk_frames.
The players' walking frames on foot ($A0-$BD), a run of six, four or three per facing.
The frame for each facing while throwing a grenade ($BE-$C5).
32 bytes read by the compare at $3E51 (values 2, 3, 4 and $FF).
How many walking frames each facing has before the cycle restarts.
How many tread steps each tank facing has (3 or 1).
Where each facing's tank frames start in tank_frames; the second eight are used when the tread moves the other way.
The tank's sprite frames ($C6-$DD), six per facing, the treads turning.

The part of move_enemies that plays a shot-down helicopter (zpa_B4 bit 7 set): sets its two sprites' frames from the tables at $3D26 and $3D35 by the step in zpa_B4, and after 15 steps takes it off the screen and clears zpa_B4. (A flying one, below, moves down a line each time and turns its rotor through frames $76-$7A.)

Every second frame (not during a coarse scroll or while zpa_2A is set), moves the soldiers; while zpa_AC is set it runs the ending's figures at $2F15 instead. Each soldier steps through its movement script: the step in $035D+x indexes enemy_moves ($B448) for its state $036D+x and enemy_times ($B4C2) for how long it lasts; a duration of $FF loops the script back. A dying soldier shows enemy_death_frames. A walking one moves one to four pixels a step in the direction of its state's low three bits, and is dropped when it leaves the play area. Its frame comes from tank_frames for a soldier in a vehicle ($03BD+x bit 7), from $6F in colour 11 when in water, or from soldier_walk_frames. Also animates the thing in zpa_B4 (a sprite at $7B4A that falls to line $F8 cycling frames $76-$7A, or that plays through heli_frames).
How many walking frames a soldier has per facing.
Where each facing's frames start in soldier_walk_frames.

The soldiers' walking frames, $51-$6E, in steps for each facing: most frames are listed twice so that each shows for two steps, and the lists for facings 3 and 5 run forward and back again, so some frames on the way back appear once.

Plays sound effect A when effects are on (bit 7 of zpa_9C), on a free voice or on the voice playing the lowest-priority effect (priorities in effect_priority); with music on (bit 6) only voice 0 is used for effects. Returns the voice in A, or $FF if none was taken. Keeps X and Y.
The priority of each of the 23 sound effects, compared by play_effect.

Reads the keyboard for F5 (row 0, column 6) when no other key and no stick on port 1 is held. Each new press of F5 steps the sound setting in zpa_9C round its four values (bits 7 and 6: music, effects): turning music off stops the driver (stop_music), turning it on restarts tune zpa_A3.
Sets zpa_AC to $FF for the ending, empties the 16 soldier slots, and puts eight figures from ending_figures on screen in colour 5; records the top row in zpa_1D.
The eight figures of the ending: X positions, then (from $2EFD) Y positions, then (from $2F05) sprite frames.
The ending figures' Y positions.
The sprite frames of the eight ending figures.
While the ending runs (zpa_AC set), move_enemies comes here instead: every 8 frames the eight ending figures switch between the two sets of frames at ending_figures+16 and +24.

Installs the game's interrupt chain: banks the ROMs out ($01=$35), points the hardware IRQ vector at irq_top ($2F65), stops CIA 1's interrupts, enables the raster interrupt for line 0 and acknowledges any pending one, and points the NMI vector at nmi_ignore ($3473) so that RESTORE does nothing. Keeps the interrupt flag as it was.

Raster interrupt at line 0, the top of the frame and the first of a chain of five. Puts the eight sprites of the top panel in place (Y $1A, X from $30 to $120, frames $10-$17, which spell PLAYER-1, HIGH and PLAYER-2, multicolour, colours 15 and 13 with shared colours 11 and 12), sets the next interrupt for line $30 at irq_panel ($3085), and writes $D011 with the fine scroll zpa_4A and both the bitmap and extended-colour bits set: an invalid mode that shows black, so the top border area shows only the sprites. It patches the value irq_play_on will write and the two delay counts (from scroll_delays) that keep its split on the same cycle whatever the fine scroll, copies the new fine scroll zpa_4B into zpa_4A, then runs prepare_sprites ($38D3), $3C1D, $3474 and $BD9C before returning.

Two tables of eight, indexed by the fine vertical scroll: the delay loop counts patched into irq_play_on ($30D0, from $3051) and irq_bottom ($31B2, from $3059), 9 except for 5 and 1 at scrolls 6 and 7, where a bad line steals the cycles instead.
The delay counts patched into irq_bottom ($31B2), by fine scroll.

Points the IRQ vector at X (low) and Y (high), acknowledges the video chip's interrupt and sets the raster compare to line A. If the beam has already passed that line, it moves the compare on a line at a time until it is ahead of the beam, so that the interrupt is never missed.
Raster interrupt at line $30: runs $355B, sets the sprites' shared colours (2 and 0, or 11 and 12 on the title screens, zpa_AA negative) and sets the next interrupt for line $46 at irq_play_on.

Raster interrupt at line $46, where the play area starts: waits for the line to pass and a patched delay, then turns the screen back into normal character mode with the current fine scroll (the patched value at $30C7). Copies the sprite pointers for the first band from $7BC5-$7BCC, adds the screen's vertical movement zpa_22 to both players' Y (zpa_1B, zpa_1C) and keeps it in zpa_21, and runs $3628 and $3614. When a coarse scroll is due (zpa_23 negative) it marks it in progress ($7F), moves the top row zpa_4C to zpa_93, moves the two screen-row pointers zpa_E8 and zpa_EA one row (40 bytes) the same way, re-enables interrupts and redraws the play area (copy_play_area); otherwise it checks the F5 key (check_f5).
The value irq_play_on writes to $D011, rewritten every frame by irq_top from the fine scroll zpa_4A (the vertical scroll bits, with the screen on and 25 rows).
The count of irq_play_on's delay loop, rewritten every frame by irq_top from scroll_delays so that the $D011 write lands at the same point of the raster line whatever the fine scroll.

Raster interrupt used for the sprite bands in the play area: ORs $01 with 5 so that the I/O block is visible even if the main code had lowered it to read RAM under I/O, then runs the multiplexer step at $3638.

Raster interrupt near the bottom of the play area (from line $EE): waits a patched delay and writes $7B to $D011, the invalid mode again, so the area below the play field shows black; blanks all eight sprite pointers ($40) and turns the sprites off, counts the frame in zpa_2F and sets the next interrupt for line $F9 at irq_lower_panel. When a scroll script is running (zpa_A7/zpa_A8), it takes the next step: adds it to the fine scroll zpa_4B and, when that crosses a character row, asks irq_play_on for a coarse scroll up or down (zpa_93, zpa_23 = $FF); a step of $7F ends the script. Then, with interrupts enabled, it moves the soldiers (move_enemies) and calls the music driver ($E000) once for each frame owed in zpa_25, unless it is already doing so.
The count of irq_bottom's delay loop, rewritten every frame by irq_top from the table after scroll_delays.

Raster interrupt at line $F9: writes $73 to $D011 (24 rows, which keeps the lower border open), puts the eight sprites of the lower panel in place (Y 2, past the bottom of the screen, X $38 to $120, colour 13, shared colours 2 and 5) and goes on to draw the panel at $3D44.

Redraws the play area from the map: patches the source addresses of the unrolled copy below with the map and colour rows for the 22 rows from the top row zpa_4C (row pointers $C87F and $C8FF, wrapping at 64), then copies 32 characters and 32 colours of each row to the screen at $4054 (column 4 of row 2) and down, and to colour RAM at $D854. The row order of the patched operands is in copy_row_order.

The source addresses of the play area's character rows in copy_play_area's unrolled LDA instructions (every 12 bytes from here, for the first 20 rows), rewritten before each copy from map_row_ptrs in the order of copy_row_order, starting at the top row zpa_4C.
The high bytes of the same addresses.
The source addresses of the play area's colour rows in copy_play_area's unrolled LDA instructions, rewritten from colour_row_ptrs (their low bytes match the character rows').
The high bytes of copy_play_area's colour-row source addresses ($0C-$13 for the colour window), each the twelfth byte after the last; the routine runs on from here through all 22 rows.
The character and colour sources of the play area's 21st row, rewritten the same way.
The high byte of the 21st row's character source.
The low byte of the 21st row's colour source.
The high byte of the 21st row's colour source.
The character and colour sources of the play area's 22nd and last row, rewritten the same way.
The high byte of the 22nd row's character source.
The low byte of the 22nd row's colour source.
The high byte of the 22nd row's colour source.
For each of the first 20 rows, the offset of its pair of operands in the unrolled copy of copy_play_area; the last two rows are patched separately.
The NMI handler: a lone RTI, so RESTORE does nothing.

The first half of the sprite multiplexer, run from irq_top. The game keeps 36 moving objects (Y at $7B48+x, 0 when unused; X $7B00+x with its ninth bit at $7B24+x; frame $7B6C+x; colour $7B90+x). Unless a coarse scroll is in progress (zpa_34 = 0, when it reuses last frame's order), it sorts them by Y with a bucket table: each object's Y halved indexes the 128 bytes at $7A80, and the object goes into the first free bucket at or up to seven below it (objects at Y $EC or more are left out). It then takes the first eight objects in bucket order for the first band of hardware sprites ($7BB4-$7BD4: X, Y, frames, colours, ninth bits, and the object numbers at $7BD5), emptying their buckets, and leaves the scan position in zpa_24 for the bands below.

Copies the first band of eight sprites prepared by sort_sprites into the video chip ($D000-$D010, $D027-$D02E), blanks the sprite pointers to frame $40 until irq_play_on sets the real ones, and enables all eight sprites in multicolour.
Points the IRQ at irq_band and schedules the first reuse of a hardware sprite (band_next, from scan position zpa_24), keeping the position in zpa_33.
Sets zpa_34 to 0 while a coarse scroll is due (zpa_23 = $FF) and to $FF otherwise; sort_sprites and the bands use it to decide whether the bucket table is rebuilt or reused.

The second half of the multiplexer, run in irq_band: takes the next objects in bucket order and gives each to the hardware sprite whose last use ended (sprite 7, then 6, down to 0 and round again) as soon as the beam is 21 lines past that sprite's Y, writing its Y, colour, X, ninth bit and frame pointer. It then schedules the next interrupt two lines before the next object's bucket, or, at the end of the list ($7F), the bottom interrupt irq_bottom at line $EE.

Finds the next object in the bucket table from position X and sets the raster interrupt for it (two lines above its bucket); if the beam is already past that line, carries on with sprite_bands at once. At the end of the list it installs irq_bottom for line $EE.
Moves every object except the players down by zpa_21, the screen's scroll in pixels this frame (1 forward, $FF back); a dead player's sprite moves too.

Q pauses the game: sets zpa_2A (which stops the soldiers, the grenades, the explosions and the players' moves in the interrupt), plays sound 22, waits for Q to be let go, then waits for fire on either joystick (carries on, A = $FF) or for @ (returns with Z set, which ends the game). The rest of the main loop stops because the loop is held inside this routine. Returns at once with A = $FF if Q is not held.

Every third frame, reads the keys that lock a player's aim: RUN/STOP or C= toggles zpa_2B, = or up-arrow toggles zpa_2A+players (zpa_2B in a one-player game, zpa_2C, player 2's, in a two-player game), each with sound 22, once per press. While a lock is on, the player keeps facing the same way while walking (see lower_panel_irq), the way the arcade's rotary joystick let a soldier run one way and fire another.
Draws 48 rows of the route (draw_rows): window rows from 32 below the top row up to 15 above it, the whole view and the rows on either side.
Draws 34 rows of the route through draw_rows, from 48 rows ahead of the top row backwards.

Draws X rows of the route into the map window, from 48 rows ahead of the top row zpa_4C backwards, one row each through draw_map_row ($7F80), then puts zpa_4C back and records it in zpa_5F, the row the drawing has reached.
When the view has caught up with the drawn rows (zpa_4C = zpa_5F), draws the next route row ($7F80) and moves zpa_5F back one row.
Every 4 frames, updates the lower panel for each player through update_panel_now.

Redraws the digits of the lower panel that have changed, per player: lives (zpa_8B-$93), bullets (zpa_6D, two BCD digits), grenades (zpa_6F) or, in a tank, shells (zpa_E0), and the two bytes of score (zpa_89, zpa_87), each digit through draw_panel_digit; then the bar of the tank's fuel (zpa_53, through draw_fuel_bar) and the high score (zpa_86, zpa_85). Each digit is drawn only when it differs from the copy kept at zpa_71-zpa_84 and zpa_C4-zpa_C7.

Draws the tank's fuel bar for player X into the panel sprite: from the value zpa_4F (0-63), writes full ($55), partial (fuel_bar_parts) and empty cells, with the bar's ends from fuel_bar_ends, into four rows of the sprite at fuel_bar_rows.
The panel sprite addresses of the fuel bar for each player, and the steps and cell offsets draw_fuel_bar uses to fill it.
The high bytes of the fuel bars' sprite addresses: $46 for player 1 and $47 for player 2, in the lower panel's sprites.

The base of a table read with X from 1 to 11, so that entry X is fuel_bar_steps' entry X-1: the fuel level at which cell X of the bar starts, subtracted from the fuel to tell how full (0-3) that cell is. The 0 here is never read.
Twelve fuel levels, 4 to 48 in steps of 4, each the point at which one more cell of the bar fills.
The four patterns of the bar's left end, from empty to full.
The four patterns of the bar's right end.
The four patterns of a cell in the middle, from empty to full ($55 is full).
The offsets in the sprite of the bar's twelve cells, three bytes a row and four rows down.
Draws digit A into the panel sprite at the place Y names (from panel_digit_pos, two more for player 2): copies the digit's eight rows from the panel font at $AC57 into every third byte of the sprite.
The sprite addresses of each digit of the lower panel, for player 1 and player 2 in pairs: lives, bullets, grenades, score, then the high score.
The high bytes of panel_digit_pos's sprite addresses, interleaved with the low bytes.

Moves the eight grenades and shells ($7B4C+x, 0 when unused) unless the game is paused or in attract mode: each counts down its flight ($0276+x); at 14 it sets off its explosion (grenade_lands); while it flies it moves two pixels a frame in its direction and is dropped at the play area's edges; its frame comes from grenade_frames (a grenade growing and shrinking as it arcs, colour 7, or colour 10 with the blast power-up) or, for a shell, the frames at $3D1F and frame $74 at the end (colour 1 or 7).
Plays sound 8 and marks grenade X's explosion as due ($0293+x = $FF).

The sprite frame for each step of a grenade's flight ($88 down to $82, then $70-$73 and back), a shell's frames from $3D1F, and two tables used by the animation in zpa_B4 (frames from $3D26, positions from $3D35).
The sprite frames of a shell's flight.
The frames of the left sprite of a shot-down helicopter, by step (animate_heli_down).
The frames of the right sprite of a shot-down helicopter, by step.

The rest of irq_lower_panel, and the place where the players move. Reads keyboard rows 7, 6 and 5 into zpa_3A-zpa_3C and the joysticks: port 2 into zpa_11 (player 2) and port 1 into zpa_10 (player 1), or both ANDed into zpa_10 in a one-player game, so either stick works. Sets the panel's sprite frames $18-$1F and the next interrupt for line $30 at irq_top. In attract mode it plays the demo's inputs ($B7A3); while paused it does nothing more. For each living player: a newly started player walks itself up from the bottom (zpa_A5 counts the time); boarding a tank runs $C70C; otherwise the stick's direction (dir_from_stick) gives the walking direction zpa_13 and, unless the aim lock zpa_2B is on, the facing zpa_31; the player is moved ($C485) unless throwing, and the walking frame advances at the pace in tbl_2B97. A dead player is handled by $C456. Then the players' sprites are placed, and the screen scrolls: forward one pixel (zpa_0C/zpa_0D up by one) when both players are above line $BC, back one pixel when one is at the bottom and the other below line $68, but never more than ten rows back from the furthest point reached (zpa_1D).

The eight sprite frames $10-$17 that make the score panel in the opened upper border: "PLAYER-1", "HIGH" and "PLAYER-2" over their scores, each score four digits drawn in by draw_panel_digit before two fixed zeros.

The eight sprite frames $18-$1F that make the status bar in the opened lower border, four for each player: lives, bullets with a gun, grenades, and the tank's fuel bar, with digits drawn in by draw_panel_digit and the bar by draw_fuel_bar.

The intro's character set as loaded, 157 characters: the scenery the opening sequence scrolls past (intro_ground). restore_charset replaces the first 87 characters with the game's own when the intro ends, and the route's tile sets and the title fonts are written over the rest as they are needed.
The last 29 characters of the intro's character set.
The intro's scenery, 12 rows of 20 characters from intro_charset, which draw_intro_rows lays across the screen twice side by side as the ground scrolls.
Zeroes at load: the end of the character set, where copy_title_font later writes the letters at $4E00 and the route its items and explosions.
Characters $C0-$CB once copy_title_font has run: the first letters of the title font.
Characters $CC-$CF, the item on the ground, whose shapes animate_items swaps every 12 frames (they are title font letters on the title screens).
Characters $E0-$EF: the space, punctuation and the rest of the title font, and in play the big explosion's last characters.
Characters $F0-$FF: the digits of the title font, and in play the big letters game_over draws "GAME OVER" with.
The last eight bytes of the character set, at $4FF8, where cold_start writes $FF; with the screen at $4000 the sprite pointers are at $43F8, so nothing reads these.
Sprite frames $41-$48: a player falling and sinking into the ground, shown by player_dying.
Sprite frames $49-$50: a soldier standing and facing each of eight directions, the frame enemy_think gives a soldier as it turns.
Sprite frames $51-$60: the soldiers running, two frames for each of the eight directions.
Sprite frames $61-$6E: more of the soldiers' running and throwing frames.
Sprite frame $6F: a soldier under water, only the ripples showing.
Sprite frames $70-$74: a grenade or shell in flight, at its sizes as it rises and falls.
Sprite frames $75-$7A: the helicopter's body, and its rotor in five positions.
Sprite frames $7B-$81: the swelling and fading cloud of a sprite explosion (start_explosion, kind 0, through explosion_frames), not the character-drawn big explosion of update_big_blasts.
Sprite frames $82-$88: a mine going off, a ring of fire.
Sprite frames $89-$8D: the letters I, K, A, R and I of the title.
Sprite frames $8E-$92: "Warriors" in script, in five pieces.

Sprite frames $93-$9F: the ending's figures, two sprites wide and four high, from the head ($93, $94) down to the boots ($99, $9A), with $9B-$9F their other steps. Only ending_figures_frames names them (ending_setup, ending_animate).
Sprite frames $A0-$AF: the player standing and walking in each direction.
Sprite frames $B0-$BF: the player walking and aiming.
Sprite frames $C0-$C5: the last of the player's frames, crouched and throwing.
Sprite frames $C6-$D5: the tank, its turret turned to each direction, the first two thirds of its frames.
Sprite frames $D6-$DD: the rest of the tank's frames.
Sprite frame $DE: the "IN" sign an empty tank flashes.
Sprite frames $DF-$E1: a burning, smoking tank.
Sprite frames $E2-$E9: a soldier wading in water, facing each of eight directions ($E2 plus the facing).

The colour of each of the 256 characters, as colour RAM values, read by draw_map_row whenever it puts a character in the map: the game's own characters' colours as loaded, then each tile set's written in by map_load_tiles. Either of bits 7 and 6 makes a character solid to anyone walking (map_cell_at); bit 6 also stops bullets and grenades (update_shots, update_grenade_hits) and bit 7 keeps items off it (drop_item); a low nibble of $E is water.

Draws the next row of the route into the map window. First runs the map script one step (map_script_step). The row goes to window row (zpa_4C - 16) AND 63: 32 characters at $0400 + row*32 and their colours at $0C00 + row*32. The ground comes first, by the fill mode zpa_D3: 0 copies the row of the 64-row ground pattern at $D800 + row*32 (RAM under I/O, read with $01 lowered), colouring each character from char_colours ($7E80); 1 copies the 16 characters at offset 8 of that pattern into both halves; 2 fills the row with character $3E in colour 14; 3 fills it with spaces in colour 9. Then every active map object (six slots, $7D09+x nonzero) draws its next row on top. An object is a stream: 0 leaves a column as it is, a byte below $38 is a character offset added to the object's tile base ($7D2D+x), a byte of $38 or more is a character as it stands, and a byte with bit 7 set repeats the next byte that many times ($80 alone ends the row). A row starting $FF calls a sub-object: the slot pushes its state (four levels in $7D15-$7D6F) and plays the object named by the next two bytes (a repeat count and an object number) until it ends. A row starting $80 ends a pass: the repeat count $7D15+x drops and the sub-object starts again, or, at zero, the slot pops back to its caller; a slot whose stack empties is free.
Starts the map script at the address in X (low) and Y (high), held in zpa_D6/zpa_D7, marks tile slot 0's base as $FF and frees all six object slots.

Runs the map script until it reaches a wait. When zpa_D7 is 0 (no game yet) it first starts the script at map_script ($92E1); when the wait counter zpa_D2 is running, it only counts down. A command byte's top three bits pick what it does: bit 7 set waits the low seven bits' number of rows more; %000 starts an object (the next byte's number) in the first free slot at the column in the low five bits (a full set of slots steps the background colour, a leftover debug sign, and takes slot 0); %001 starts one in the slot the low bits name, at the column in the next byte; %011 runs a special command (map_special); anything else loads a set of characters (map_load_tiles).

The map script's special commands, by the low five bits: $10 sets the background colours $D021-$D023 from the next three bytes (skipped in attract mode, zpa_AB); $0F starts the ending (ending_setup); $0E sets zpa_AD, which sends the main loop to route_finished; $11 sends a helicopter down the screen (unless one is already flying, zpa_B4, or in attract mode): sound 14, two sprites side by side at the X the next byte gives times 2, line $30, frames $75 and $76 in colours 5 and 15, the second its turning rotor; $12 sets the soldiers' fire_chance from the next byte; $13 adds a stretch of breakable scenery to the blast list ($7DC3, six slots: column, width, height, and the two bytes the rubble uses); $14 adds a gun position to the gun list ($7DCF, four slots: its column, then its kind, recorded at the current row); $1C-$1F set the ground's fill mode zpa_D3 from the low two bits. Other values do nothing.

Loads a tile set: the low five bits name the tile slot, the next byte the first character it fills (stored less one in tile_bases, $7CE5+slot), then the address of its character shapes and the address of its colour list. The colour list's first byte is the count of characters; their colours go into char_colours ($7E80) and their shapes, 8 bytes each, into the game's character set at $4800.
The address of each map object's stream, by object number (118 words). Objects 0-35 are in RAM under I/O at $D000-$D7BE, the rest at $8561-$9084.
The high bytes of map_object_ptrs, read one byte on.
For each map object, the tile slot whose base character its offsets are counted from.
Map object 36: 7 columns wide and 7 rows high, its offsets counted from tile slot 8. The route places it 5 times, first at row 151, column 11.
Map object 37 and 38: 13 columns wide and 5 rows high, one stream drawn with two tile slots (9, 1). The route places it 3 times, first at row 170, column 0.
Map object 39: 16 columns wide and 7 rows high, drawn from the game's own characters (tile slot 0). The route places it 3 times, first at row 238, column 16.
Map object 40: 32 columns wide and 6 rows high, its offsets counted from tile slot 3. Used only inside objects 4 and 41, which call it with a repeat count.
Map object 41: 32 columns wide and 10 rows high, its offsets counted from tile slot 3. The route places it twice, first at row 589, column 0.
Map object 42: 11 columns wide and 3 rows high, drawn from the game's own characters (tile slot 0). The route places it 3 times, first at row 496, column 8, and object 51 use it as a part.

Every bullet is then tested against the players: a player on foot, not the one who fired it and not still arriving (zpa_A5), within 5 by 10 pixels dies (kill_player). A player in a tank is never hit by bullets.

Every 2 frames while the helicopter is flying (zpa_B4), keeps its sound going and, between lines $50 and $E0, one time in four fires a bullet in a random direction from it into a free enemy bullet slot (6-14).

Returns a pseudo-random byte in A. Walks player X into the tank they are boarding ($020E+y): each call steps the X position and the row one towards the tank's, so the player moves diagonally; once both match, takes the tank over: its fuel, shells and countdown pass to the player (zpa_53, zpf_E0, zpf_CA), zpa_36 is set, sound 6 plays and the tank shudders (zpa_5B = $80).

Reached when the map script has raised zpa_AD: winds the game down (wind_down), gives each player who still has lives 20 times 5,000 points (100,000, keeping the lives an extra-life score would add), clears the soldiers and objects, prints ending_text and lets the ending's figures run about ten seconds, then waits for fire and goes on to the end of the game at game_over.

Plays tune 1, builds the big letters of "GAME OVER" in characters $F0-$F7 from the font at $AAD7 (game_over_letters), and flashes them on a row of the play area (game_over_row) for 200 frames, until the helicopter has gone. Throws a grenade (or, with bit 7 of A, a shell) from soldier X into a free slot among 4-7, unless fire_chance is 0: its flight time from grenade_range for the soldier's facing, its start from grenade_start_x and grenade_start_y. Returns the carry set when no slot is free.

Ends play: marks both players dead, zeroes the first byte of fire_chance (which stops the soldiers' grenades and shells, though soldiers of kinds 1-3 can still fire bullets), and keeps the game's routines running until every bullet, grenade and big explosion has finished; then updates the panel.

Moves the big explosion on a step: erases each arm (putting back what was beneath), moves it one cell outward, and drops arms that leave the window. After seven steps the explosion is over (zpa_EF = 0).

The music driver's once-a-frame entry, called from the interrupt (intro_irq during the intro, the lower panel's interrupt in play). Keeps zpa_F8-zpa_FA. When a tune is playing (music_on), counts down the tempo (step_count): every so many frames it reads the next event of each of the three voices (voice_step), and every frame it updates each voice's sound (voice_update). Then it runs the sound effects (effect_update) and sets the volume ($D418) to 15, or to the value the tune last chose (volume).
The operand of an LDA #: 0 while no tune plays, which skips the music; start_tune sets it.

The operand of another LDA #, always 0 in this game: when set, the driver would skip every sixth frame, the usual way of making music written for one television standard play at the same speed on the other. Nothing writes it.
The operand of the LDA # that reloads the step counter: the frames between events, set from the tune table by start_tune (4, 5 or 6).
The operand of the LDA # written to $D418 every frame, changed by the tune's volume command.
Two unused bytes between the driver's frame routine and start_effect_voice.

Copies the 20-byte definition of sound effect A (effect_table, $EB34 plus 20 times A) into voice X's effect slots ($E5BC-$E5F5 in steps of three) and marks the voice as taken by an effect ($E5FE+x = $FF), so the music leaves it alone until the effect ends. Called by play_effect.
The operand of the ADC # inside start_effect_voice, rewritten with the effect number times two, so that the routine can make the number times twenty.

The address in start_effect_voice's LDA $FFFF,Y, rewritten with the effect's definition. The low bytes here and at $E08F also happen to be where the event loop's table of commands is indexed from: an event byte of $80-$8E, used as an index from $E080 and $E08F, reads music_commands at $E100 and $E10F.
The high byte of the effect's address.
The rest of start_effect_voice: starts the effect's step and sweep counters.

Starts tune A (0 for the title, 1 for game over, 2 in play): silences the chip (stop_music), clears the driver's state ($E55C-$E5B8), sets the frame counter, and from the tune's seven bytes in tune_table takes the tempo and, for each voice, the address of its pattern list ($E565/$E568) and its first pattern, read through the rewritten LDA instructions at $E0DF and $E0E5. Then turns the music on.
The address in start_tune's first LDA $FFFF, rewritten with the voice's pattern list, to read the first pattern's low byte.
Its high byte.
The address in the second LDA $FFFF, one byte further on, for the first pattern's high byte.
The high byte of the second address, for reading a voice's first pattern's high byte.

The addresses, less one, of the routines for the tune's command bytes $80 to $8E, low bytes then high bytes ($E10F), pushed and returned to by voice_step: $80 a rest, $81 vibrato off, $82 volume, $83 a slide by a 16-bit step, $84 and $85 bend the note down and up, $86 the end of a pattern, $87 vibrato on, $88 drum mode, $89 pulse width, $8A pulse sweep, $8B stop the music, $8C transpose, $8D an unused value (stored at $E603 and never read), $8E a tied note.
Command $8B: drops the return address, turns the voice off and stops the music (stop_music_a with 0).
Stops the music and the effects, and silences the sound chip by clearing $D400-$D417.
The same, storing A as the music_on flag.
Command $8A: a pulse width that sweeps between two limits by a step (three bytes).
Command $83: sets the voice's slide flag, the 16-bit step, and a delay in frames before the slide starts (three bytes); after the delay voice_update adds the step every frame.
Command $86, the end of a pattern: moves on to the voice's next pattern in its pattern list; a 0 there starts the list again from the top, so every tune loops.

Command $8E: adds one to the voice's flags ($E55C+x), setting bit 0, so that the next note starts with its gate already on. Normally a note's first frame is written with the gate off, which lets the envelope start again; a tied note runs on from the last.
Command $8D: stores a byte at $E603, which nothing reads.
Command $8C: the voice's transposition in semitones ($E5B0+x).
Command $89: a fixed pulse width, sweep off.
Command $87: vibrato depth and speed.
Command $85: bends each note up (flag bits $C0).
Command $84: bends each note down (flag bit $40).
Command $81: turns the vibrato off.
Command $82: sets the volume (volume).
Command $88: drum mode (flag bits 1 and 2): voice_update then alternates the voice every frame between noise, higher up, and its own waveform.
voice_step for the next voice.

Reads the next events of voice X's pattern when its note has run out ($E583+x): bytes $E0-$FF set the length of the notes that follow (the low five bits plus one, in steps of the tempo); $D0-$DF choose an instrument (a waveform from waveforms, then the attack/decay and sustain/release bytes); $C0-$CF choose an arpeggio (arp_starts); $80-$8E are commands (music_commands); a byte below $80 is a note, which starts with the gate on and is written to the chip unless an effect holds the voice. While a note sounds, the bend flags move its pitch a semitone a step.
voice_update for the next voice.

Works out voice X's frequency each frame: the note plus the arpeggio's offset (arp_table, stepping each frame and looping where an entry has bit 7 set) plus the transposition, through freq_table; adds vibrato (a triangle of the given depth and speed), the slide, and the pulse sweep; then writes frequency, pulse width and control to the chip, unless an effect holds the voice. Flag bit 2 flips every frame; in drum mode the frames with it set play noise ($81). It then adds $31 to its copy of the frequency's high byte, after the frequency was written, so that raise never reaches the chip.
effect_update for the next voice.

Runs the sound effect on voice X, if one holds it: on its first frame writes its envelope and pulse width; then each frame counts down its length (silencing the voice and freeing it at the end), sweeps its frequency by one of two steps chosen by a rotating bit pattern, adds its main step, jumps back to its start frequency every so many frames, and alternates between two waveforms by another bit pattern.
The four waveforms an instrument can choose: noise ($80), pulse ($40), sawtooth ($20) and triangle ($10).
The sound chip's frequency for each of 84 notes, seven octaves of semitones (low byte first).
The high bytes of freq_table, read one byte on.
One byte into freq_table's 33rd note, which starts at $E4F4: the high byte of that note's frequency.

The offset of each voice's registers in the sound chip, 0, 7 and 14, loaded with the game and never written: voice_update, voice_step and effect_update read it with the voice in X (LDY voice_regs,X) to write that voice's frequency, pulse width and control.
